title: Write it out
hookLine: James Pennebaker's studies: writing about hard things for a few days helped many people
last: TAKE IT FOR A WALK SOMEWHERE GREEN.

cards: A thing never told to anyone can sit in a person like a stone in a shoe. Maybe it's big, maybe it's small and just embarrassing. People get used to walking on it.
In the 1980s a young psychologist in Texas, James Pennebaker, wondered what carrying a secret like that does to a person, and what happens if they set it down. Not by telling anyone. Not by therapy.
Just by writing about it, for a few minutes, on a few days, for no audience. It sounded too simple to matter.

teach.b: In 1986 Pennebaker and Sandra Beall asked college students to write for about fifteen minutes a day, four days in a row.
Some wrote about the most upsetting experience of their lives, their deepest thoughts and feelings about it. Others wrote about ordinary things, like their room or their shoes.

teach.h: WORSE AT FIRST, FEWER VISITS LATER.
teach.b: Right after writing, the first group often felt worse, so this isn't instant relief. But over the following months, they visited the campus health center less often than the others.
Many more studies followed, with students, patients and others, and one large review pooled well over a hundred of them.
Reviews have found the effects real but modest, and they vary: it helps some people clearly and others barely at all. Compared to what, and no magic. Why might it work?

Pennebaker noticed that the people who seemed to benefit most gradually began to tell a story, using more words like because and realize over the days. The writing seemed to turn a jumble into something with a shape.
The idea isn't new. Marcus Aurelius's Meditations read as private notes, written to himself, and the Psalms are full of honest complaint put into words.
You don't have to keep what you write: in his advice for readers, Pennebaker says the pages can be thrown away.
The point isn't a finished piece. It's getting the stone out of the shoe and looking at it.
One caution, from day three hundred seven: if writing brings up more than you can hold, stop, and talk to someone you trust or a professional.

how: In expressive writing, based on James Pennebaker's research, people write privately about a difficult experience for about fifteen to twenty minutes on three or four days, and often throw the pages away.

o: the psychologist who studied writing privately about hard things
the therapist who had patients read their diaries aloud
a scholar who studied Marcus Aurelius's private notes

games.q: writing it out — tap the pairs.

s: expressive writing makes you feel better right away
people often felt worse right after; the benefits showed up later.
you have to keep what you write, or share it
Pennebaker's advice for readers is that the pages can be thrown away.
the effects of expressive writing are real but modest

games.q: you write about something painful and feel worse afterward. what did the early studies find?
o: that means it's harmful: never do it.
feeling worse right after was common; benefits came later.
games.why: the writers often felt worse at first, then visited the health center less in the months after. and if it's too much, it's okay to stop.

practice: With a pen and any scrap of paper, or a note you'll delete, write about something that's been weighing on you: what happened and how it felt, without fixing grammar or making it nice.
When you're done, throw it away or delete it, and if it gets too heavy, stop.

wordCard.voice: Pennebaker, who found that putting a hard thing into words for a few short sessions, for no reader, brings modest but real benefits.

carryVoice: Your line: the stone in your shoe. Nobody needs to read the page, not even you. That's day three hundred eighteen.
